newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Netanyahu exchange views on Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Netanyahu exchange views on Mideast.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rebuffed his call for a U.S.-led Mideast summit, saying the current process offers the best hope for peace.

Tough talk by both Clinton and Netanyahu before their meeting reflected the difficulties they face trying to keep an outbreak of violence over new Jewish settlements from completely derailing the Israeli-Palestinian peace process

At the start of the Oval Office talks, Clinton said that Netanyahu's suggestion for U.S.-led Camp David-style talks was premature -- while the Israeli leader made clear even before going to the White House that he would not reverse his decision to build new settlements.
"I think it is very important to get this peace process back on track," Clinton told reporters assembled to witness the opening of the talks.
"I think its important that we not put form over substance here," Clinton said. "Its important to know where we're going and thats what I want to talk to the prime minister about."
The meeting lasted about two hours and Netanyahu left without making any comment to White House reporters. He had a news conference scheduled for later in the day.
The urgency of their meeting was underscored by yet more violence on the West Bank, where a Jewish settler shot and wounded at least two Palestinians during a stone-throwing incident on Monday.

Clashes have erupted nearly every day since Israel broke ground last month on Har Homa, a 6,500-home project on a hilltop in East Jerusalem that Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim and on land each side claims.
The White House said Clinton had some new ideas to offer at the meeting, which was hastily arranged after the Middle East peace process crumbled in the last few weeks.

As a follow up to Clinton's diplomatic efforts, administration officials say Secretary of State Madeleine Albright may be dispatched to the region. A senior Palestinian delegation is to meet Clinton later this week.

Clinton, when asked about Netanyahu's suggestion that it might require a summit like the one at Camp David that was convened by President Jimmy Carter in 1978, replied: "It's important not to jump the gun on that."
"The first thing we have to do is get the process going again," Clinton said. "There is a pre-existing process."

Netanyahu has proposed that he and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat reach a final peace agreement within six months, and said the goal may require an intensive three-way summit like the one that led to accords between Egypt and Israel.

During the Camp David negotiations, Carter most often met separately with Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Egyptian President Anwar Sadat -- pressuring each one to move closer to the position of the other.
U.S. officials made clear Clinton was resisting Israeli pressure to take that sort of role in the stalled talks.

Before his session with Clinton, Netanyahu generated thunderous applause from a pro-Israeli American group when he scornfully dismissed those who challenged "our right to build apartments" in mainly Arab East Jerusalem.

Netanyahu scoffed at Palestinian condemnation of the project. "This simple act has been described as terrorism -- the terrorism of the walk-up rentals, the terrorism of the condominiums," he said to laughter from a packed meeting room.
The United States opposes all new Israeli settlements in the disputed territory, but has muted its public criticism in hopes of finding a way to defuse tensions.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry played down notions that any dramatic announcement was at hand. "This is a work in progress, and will be a work in progress," he said, noting that a senior Palestinian delegation would meet with Clinton later this week.
He and other U.S. officials underscored the point that Clinton resisting pressure for the United States to intervene more forcefully in the stalled Israeli-Palestinian talks.

Middle East envoy Dennis Ross told the American Israel Public Affairs Committee: "Neither the U.S. nor anyone else is going to impose a settlement." He added: "Obviously, we have a role to help, but we can not impose an outcome ... we can't wave a magic wand and put things back on track."
